title: SE POC model tuning checklist and notes
body:
Purpose and audience:
This is a pragmatic, checklist-style note for Solutions Engineering POCs where we need to pick model variants, choose a quantization path, and iterate on prompt/pipeline tuning. Intended for SEs running short (1–4 week) technical POCs with customers who care about a mix of latency, accuracy, and cost.

POC goals and metrics (template):
- Primary goal: e.g., "achieve customer intent-detection F1 >= 0.88 at avg token latency <= 120ms and cost < $X/1k tokens".
- Key metrics to track: latency p50/p95, throughput (tokens/s), per-1k-token cost estimate, task-specific accuracy/EM/F1, hallucination count on eval set, memory footprints (GPU RAM), tokenization overhead.
- Dataset: baseline dev/test split + 200–500 hard examples collected from customer (red-team).
- SLAs: define latency SLO and allowed tail latency.

Model selection quick guide:
- Low-latency, low-cost experiments (edge-like): Mistral-7B/Alpaca-style distilled 7B variants or Llama2-7B-int8 where available. Favor models with shorter quantized kernels and proven 8-bit runtimes.
- Balanced quality/latency: Llama-2-13B, Mistral-7B-variant (higher-quality), or Falcon-2-7B/13B depending on instruction-following.
- High-quality, higher cost: Falcon-40B / Llama2-70B (hosted or Dedicated). Use only if customer requires high reasoning/long-context.
- Consider model tokenizer: some tokenizers have higher average tokens per sentence which affects cost and latency. Test tokens-per-message early.

Quantization strategy (practical path):
1) Baseline: run FP16 on a small sample to get best-quality reference (hosted or dedicated).
2) Q4/NF4/INT8 experiments: pick 1–2 quant methods supported by runtime (e.g., nf4/q4_0/awq). Run accuracy vs. speed sweep.
3) AWQ/LLM.int8 hybrid: useful when 4-bit methods drop quality on certain heads — test HF checkpoint + awq requant.
4) Per-layer sensitivity: if quality drops, run a small sensitivity pass to keep a few causal layers in FP16 (mixed-precision).
5) Final: prefer the lowest-bit config that meets accuracy threshold; document memory and kernel characteristics (CUDA kernels, flash attention compatibility).

Serving/runtime notes relevant to Redwood platform:
- Use KV cache for multi-turn and prompt-chunk reuse. Measure warm-start vs cold-start latency.
- Leverage automatic batching but set max_batch_size to meet p95 SLOs. Start with conservative batch cap (4–8) then tune.
- Cache prefix for static system+instruction text to cut token cost.
- Test routing/fallback: define policy to fallback to a higher-cost model for long prompts or when quality regression detected.

Prompt/pipeline tuning checklist:
- Start with a short system instruction (1–3 lines) + 1–3 few-shot examples for tricky tasks. Keep context window headroom for user input.
- Template examples: role markers (System:, User:, Assistant:) usually help. For structured outputs prefer JSON schema examples and explicit "return exactly JSON" phrasing.
- Temperature/decoding: for deterministic tasks use temperature=0 and TopP=0. For exploration tasks keep temp 0.2–0.6.
- Token limits: set max_new_tokens conservatively (estimate from average expected completion). Track truncation rate.
- Reranking/ensemble: for high-accuracy POCs, consider 3-shot sampled outputs + a small ranking model (embedding similarity or a low-cost LM reranker).

Evaluation harness and signals:
- Always run an automatic eval harness against the holdout: compute task metric (accuracy/F1/EM), hallucination rate, and calibration (confidence vs correctness).
- Profile latency with realistic payloads (median message length and worst-case long messages). Record cold-start and warm-start.
- Cost model: tokens_per_request * model_price + infra overhead. Produce a simple per-10k-requests monthlyized estimate.

Example config snippets (conceptual):
- Serving config to improve latency:
  - max_batch_size: 8
  - batching_window_ms: 8
  - enable_prefix_cache: true
  - max_concurrent_requests: 64
- Quant sweep plan:
  - run fp16 baseline on 200 examples
  - run q4_0 and nf4 on same set, record delta metrics
  - if q4_0 fails quality, try awq int8 hybrid with top-2 layers in fp16

Common gotchas and troubleshooting notes:
- Tokenization mismatches: vendor checkpoints sometimes re-tokenize. Always compare tokens-per-message between model variants.
- Long context failures: some quantized kernels allocate less scratch memory; if OOMs occur, reduce batch or use mixed precision.
- Determinism differences: quantization + sampling randomness can affect reranker reproducibility. Pin seeds for eval runs.
- Unexpected hallucinations after quantization: create a small set of regression prompts (10–20) to gate deploys.

Customer-ready deliverables from a 2-week POC:
- Short report (1–2 pages): chosen model variant, quantization setting, latency/throughput/cost, top-line accuracy, risks and recommended next steps.
- Config bundle: runtime config, prompt templates, rollout policy (canary % and fallback model).
- Eval notebook: scripts to reproduce the eval and tokenization checks.

Decision matrix (one-line heuristics):
- If p95 latency target <200ms and budget tight -> try 7B quantized (nf4/awq).
- If accuracy is primary and context <4k tokens -> try 13B in FP16 or q4 mixed; prefer Dedicated capacity for predictable tail.
- If long context (>=32k) or multi-hop reasoning -> consider larger models or a hybrid pipeline with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) + smaller LLM for synthesis.

Action items before customer demo:
- Run tokenization check on 50 representative customer messages.
- Generate 3 baseline outputs (FP16) and 3 quantized outputs; check for qualitative regressions.
- Run latency profile for 1k requests with target batch config.
- Document fallback path and emergency rollback steps.

Notes and open questions (for SE collaboration):
- Need quick reference for which models in our catalog currently support awq vs nf4 on Redwood Dedicated. Action: ask Applied ML to produce one-line table.
- Determine default recommended batch/window for low-latency enterprise demos.

Contact/ownership: Marcus Chen (solutions-engineering). Please tag in SE Slack #poc-runbook when you fork this document.
